title: Module 12 Challenge: Why Does the Correlation Look Weak?
scenario: A selective graduate program admits only applicants who score in the top 15 percent on an entrance exam. The program's researchers find a correlation of r = .12 between exam score and first year grades among admitted students. A faculty member says the exam "clearly doesn't predict success, so we should drop it." In a nationwide sample of all applicants, a validation study found r = .58 between exam scores and first year grades.

parts.q: What proportion of grade variability does the national correlation of .58 account for?
What is the best explanation for the weak correlation within the program?
parts.why: Only high scorers were admitted, so exam scores vary very little among them.

parts.q: Respond to the faculty member. Explain in plain language why r = .12 in the program can coexist with r = .58 nationally, what a scatterplot would help you see, and what you would check before dropping the exam.
parts.model: Among admitted students, exam scores are bunched at the top of the scale. When X varies so little, the cloud of points is short and wide, and r shrinks even if the exam predicts well across the full range. The national sample includes low, middle, and high scorers, so the trend is easy to see there (r = .58, r squared = .34). A scatterplot of the admitted students would show a narrow band of scores with a weak tilt, while the national plot would show a clearer rise. Before dropping the exam I would correct for range restriction or compare grade outcomes for admitted students across score bands, check the reliability of the grade measure, and look for outliers. I would also ask whether the exam is the only reason students were admitted. If so, the grades of rejected applicants cannot be observed.
check: I named range restriction and explained it
I contrasted what the plots would show
I proposed checks such as reliability or outliers
I avoided concluding that the exam does not predict
